title: QT-Net: Rethinking Evaluation of AI Models in Atomic Chemical Space
claim: A staged pipeline splits data by held-out environments, compares models under cross-validation, then evaluates only on unseen cases and downstream inference.
layout: 3 colored panels left-to-right, with example molecules and formulas along the bottom
description: A wide figure with three rounded, pastel-colored panels running left to right, linked by black arrows. The first panel, 'Atomic environment split', shows a database icon (AIMEl) feeding into a SOAP/HDBSCAN clustering box with a colorful scatter of clusters. The second panel, 'Model comparison', shows a 5x5 CV fold diagram and a white box of small graph icons for the equivariant and non-equivariant models. The third panel, 'Evaluation & inference', shows a parity scatter plot (CCC & Tukey) and a 3D molecule with a dipole arrow. Below the panels, a QM9 database icon and a 'Held-out environments' label lead to two ball-and-stick test molecules. Green circles mark the held-out atoms. Summation symbols connect these molecules to the evaluation panels, including the dipole equation μ = Σ μ_i. The eye goes first to the three bold panel titles.
caption: QT-Net training and evaluation pipeline on AIMEl for atomic (QTAIM) property prediction. The molecules at the bottom are sample molecules from the test set (left: N=C1OC=CN=C1; right: N=CNC(=O)C=O), where the circled atoms are in environments held-out from training and are the only ones contributing to the scores. abstract: Atomic properties such as partial charges or multipoles encode chemically meaningful information that can inform downstream molecular property prediction, but their evaluation as machine learning targets has been complicated by the absence of a principled out-of-distribution evaluation protocol at the atomic level. In this work, we propose a held-out evaluation protocol that clusters atomic environments by SOAP descriptors and computes metrics accounting only for cluster labels unseen during training. Following this procedure, we use 5$\times$5 cross-validation and Tukey's HSD to run a statistically rigorous comparison of E(3)-equivariant against non-equivariant, rotationally augmented models for predicting electron populations and multipoles of H, C, N, and O atoms. Building on our results, we introduce the Quantum Topological Neural Network (QT-Net), a rotationally augmented, non-equivariant graph neural network. We show that QT-Net can be used to infer properties of atoms in molecules from QM9 outside our training set, and that the atomic environments seen during training strongly affect the performance of molecular property prediction tasks. To further validate the framework, molecular dipole moments computed from QT-Net's per-atom outputs recover the ground-truth values reported in QM9. We release all code and data, including a JAX implementation of QT-Net.
